1.pericope_label: Then Eliashib the high priest rose up with his brethren the priests, and they builded the sheep gate; they sanctified it, and set up the doors of it; even unto the tower of Meah they sanctified it, unto the tower of Hananeel. And next unto him builded the men of Jericho. And next to them builded Zaccur the son of Imri.

schools.summary: Delitzsch establishes that the chapter follows the course of the wall, since each party is said to build next to the one named before, so the gates stand in their real order; Ellicott adds that the formula does honour to the high priest where it first appears and takes the sanctifying as an earnest of the later consecration of the whole wall.
Gill identifies Eliashib as Jeshua's grandson and notes that in rising first he set the example, and that the men of Jericho began exactly where the priests left off.

Wesley faces the alternative sense of sanctified, that it means only prepared or repaired, and rejects it on two grounds; Clarke argues that the gate by which sacrifices entered had to be set apart for that use alone.
Henry makes the priests' precedence a rule for ministers, offers three reasons for the sanctifying, and observes that many of the builders were not inhabitants of Jerusalem at all.

debates.question: What does it mean that they sanctified the sheep gate?

positions.position: Possibly only that they prepared or repaired it, though the consecrating sense is commoner and the word is used here alone
Consecrated, for one of three reasons: it led to the temple, the work began there, or the priests built it
Set apart for the entry of sacrifices and for no other use
An earnest of the consecration of the whole wall later on

outliers.claim: Infers from the constant next-to formula that the gates are named in the order they actually stood in the wall, making the chapter a circuit rather than a catalogue.

themes: Then Eliashib the high priest rose up with his brethren the priests, and they builded the sheep gate; they sanctified it, and set up the doors of it; even unto the tower of Meah they sanctified it, unto the tower of Hananeel.
And next unto him builded the men of Jericho. And next to them builded Zaccur the son of Imri.

3.pericope_label: But the fish gate did the sons of Hassenaah build, who also laid the beams thereof, and set up the doors thereof, the locks thereof, and the bars thereof. And next unto them repaired Meremoth the son of Urijah, the son of Koz. And next unto them repaired Meshullam the son of Berechiah, the son of Meshezabeel. And next unto them repaired Zadok the son of Baana. And next unto them the Tekoites repaired; but their nobles put not their necks to the work of their Lord.

schools.summary: Delitzsch derives the fish gate's name from the market beside it, to which Syrians brought sea fish, and places it west of the corner tower in the north wall against Thenius; Ellicott sends the fish in from the Jordan and Galilee, separates the crossbars from the catches that hold them, and confirms from the Hebrew that repaired is literally strengthened.

Gill canvasses the placings of the fish gate and prefers a westward one toward the Mediterranean, and observes that the change from built to repaired is exact, the wall there having been weakened rather than demolished.

Clarke refuses the whole topographical exercise, holding that all plans of Jerusalem are works of conjecture; Wesley allows three motives for the Tekoite nobles' refusal and notes that they are branded to all posterity.

debates.question: Where did the fish gate stand and where did its fish come from?

positions.position: Westward, toward the Mediterranean, Tyre and Joppa
From the Jordan and Galilee
In the north wall, west of the corner tower, with Syrians bringing sea fish to the market beside it
Unknowable: we know scarcely anything about these gates, and all plans of the city are conjecture

outliers.claim: Rebukes the confidence of the topographers outright, asking how learnedly some men have written on subjects about which nothing is actually known.

themes: But the fish gate did the sons of Hassenaah build, who also laid the beams thereof, and set up the doors thereof, the locks thereof, and the bars thereof.

And next unto them repaired Meremoth the son of Urijah, the son of Koz. And next unto them repaired Meshullam the son of Berechiah, the son of Meshezabeel. And next unto them repaired Zadok the son of Baana.
And next unto them the Tekoites repaired; but their nobles put not their necks to the work of their Lord.

6.pericope_label: Moreover the old gate repaired Jehoiada the son of Paseah, and Meshullam the son of Besodeiah; they laid the beams thereof, and set up the doors thereof, and the locks thereof, and the bars thereof. And next unto them repaired Melatiah the Gibeonite, and Jadon the Meronothite, the men of Gibeon, and of Mizpah, unto the throne of the governor on this side the river. Next unto him repaired Uzziel the son of Harhaiah, of the goldsmiths. Next unto him also repaired Hananiah the son of one of the apothecaries, and they fortified Jerusalem unto the broad wall. And next unto them repaired Rephaiah the son of Hur, the ruler of the half part of Jerusalem.

schools.summary: Delitzsch reports the throne clause as questionable and gives Bertheau's construction under which it describes the builders rather than a landmark, settles the broad wall as a named stretch against Bertheau, and places the halved district rather than the halved city; Ellicott proposes the Damascus gate for the old gate, takes the verb rendered fortified in its literal sense of left, and notes the chapter's silence about rebuilding the gate of Ephraim.
Gill lists four identifications of the old gate without settling, and takes the rulers to have governed halves of the city itself.

Clarke reads the throne as the governor's residence and judgment seat, notes the change from Persian deputy to native governors after Nehemiah, and confirms that the trades were incorporated companies; Wesley compares the division of Jerusalem to the regions of Rome.

debates.question: Is the throne of the governor a landmark on the wall or a description of the builders?

positions.position: A landmark: the residence where the Persian governor lodged and judged
Possibly a description of the men, as belonging to the governor's seat, recording that Jews outside Nehemiah's jurisdiction came to work

debates.question: What was halved under the rulers of half parts?

positions.position: The city itself, one portion to Judah and one to Benjamin
Not the city but the district of country belonging to it

outliers.claim: Argues from silence that the gate of Ephraim, standing in a stretch the builders left untouched, is never said to have been rebuilt at all.

themes: Moreover the old gate repaired Jehoiada the son of Paseah, and Meshullam the son of Besodeiah; they laid the beams thereof, and set up the doors thereof, and the locks thereof, and the bars thereof.
And next unto them repaired Melatiah the Gibeonite, and Jadon the Meronothite, the men of Gibeon, and of Mizpah, unto the throne of the governor on this side the river.
Next unto him repaired Uzziel the son of Harhaiah, of the goldsmiths. Next unto him also repaired Hananiah the son of one of the apothecaries, and they fortified Jerusalem unto the broad wall.
And next unto them repaired Rephaiah the son of Hur, the ruler of the half part of Jerusalem.

10.pericope_label: And next unto them repaired Jedaiah the son of Harumaph, even over against his house. And next unto him repaired Hattush the son of Hashabniah. Malchijah the son of Harim, and Hashub the son of Pahath–moab, repaired the other piece, and the tower of the furnaces. And next unto him repaired Shallum the son of Halohesh, the ruler of the half part of Jerusalem, he and his daughters.

schools.summary: Delitzsch reports Bertheau's argument that a second measure implies a lost first and that the text is therefore incomplete, and rules out reading the daughters as the villages of the district on the pronoun; Ellicott declines the textual inference and calls the reading of daughters as villages needless.
Gill reads repairing opposite one's own house as sensible self-interest, and passes on Ben Melech's two derivations of Hallohesh.

Clarke suspects the arrangement was an imposed obligation on the principal people rather than a coincidence, and gives the enchanter derivation only; Wesley supposes Shallum's daughters heiresses or rich widows.
Henry takes the daughters to have contributed money for materials and wages rather than personal labour, and sets them beside the women who laboured with Paul in the gospel.

debates.question: Does the other piece imply that part of the text has been lost?

positions.position: Yes: a second measure presupposes a first, so statements about the gate of Ephraim have dropped out
No: the phrase often occurs with no earlier portion named and means only a second measure against what was just described

debates.question: Who or what were Shallum's daughters?

positions.position: Literal daughters; the villages reading is excluded by the pronoun
Literal daughters, doing voluntarily what women were not pressed to do
Heiresses or rich widows who funded the work rather than labouring on it

outliers.claim: Suggests that repairing the wall opposite one's own house was an obligation laid on the principal citizens, and perhaps the general rule of the whole work.

themes: And next unto them repaired Jedaiah the son of Harumaph, even over against his house. And next unto him repaired Hattush the son of Hashabniah.
Malchijah the son of Harim, and Hashub the son of Pahath–moab, repaired the other piece, and the tower of the furnaces.
And next unto him repaired Shallum the son of Halohesh, the ruler of the half part of Jerusalem, he and his daughters.

13.pericope_label: The valley gate repaired Hanun, and the inhabitants of Zanoah; they built it, and set up the doors thereof, the locks thereof, and the bars thereof, and a thousand cubits on the wall unto the dung gate. But the dung gate repaired Malchiah the son of Rechab, the ruler of part of Beth–haccerem; he built it, and set up the doors thereof, the locks thereof, and the bars thereof. But the gate of the fountain repaired Shallun the son of Col–hozeh, the ruler of part of Mizpah; he built it, and covered it, and set up the doors thereof, the locks thereof, and the bars thereof, and the wall of the pool of Siloah by the king’s garden, and unto the stairs that go down from the city of David.

schools.summary: Delitzsch places the valley gate near the modern Jaffa gate on Tobler's authority, locates Zanoah west of the city, keeps the thousand cubits governed by the main verb against Bertheau, and derives the covering verb from a root meaning to shade; Ellicott reads the thousand cubits as a measure of lesser damage, settles the Rechab question on the article, identifies the pool with the earlier king's pool, and admits the course of the wall becomes very hard to trace from here.
Gill raises and then abandons the possibility that the builder was a Rechabite, noting that the order was forbidden houses but might still build public defences.

Clarke places Zanoah in Judah, identifies the pool with the one the evangelists mention, and explains the stairs by the city's uneven ground; Wesley treats Beth-haccerem as a town or territory whose government was divided between two men.

debates.question: Was Malchiah the son of Rechab a Rechabite?

positions.position: Probably not, though a Rechabite forbidden houses might still build walls for the public safety
No: the text says the son of Rechab, not a son of Rechab, so it is a patronymic

debates.question: What does the thousand cubits record?

positions.position: A stretch strengthened rather than built, which had suffered less and needed less
A length still governed by the verb of the verse, against Bertheau's attempt to detach it

outliers.claim: Explains the stairs down from the city of David by the unevenness of the ground, with hills taken inside the walls, comparing the stepped streets of Bristol.

themes: The valley gate repaired Hanun, and the inhabitants of Zanoah; they built it, and set up the doors thereof, the locks thereof, and the bars thereof, and a thousand cubits on the wall unto the dung gate.
But the dung gate repaired Malchiah the son of Rechab, the ruler of part of Beth–haccerem; he built it, and set up the doors thereof, the locks thereof, and the bars thereof.

But the gate of the fountain repaired Shallun the son of Col–hozeh, the ruler of part of Mizpah; he built it, and covered it, and set up the doors thereof, the locks thereof, and the bars thereof, and the wall of the pool of Siloah by the king’s garden, and unto the stairs that go down from the city of David.

16.pericope_label: After him repaired Nehemiah the son of Azbuk, the ruler of the half part of Beth–zur, unto the place over against the sepulchres of David, and to the pool that was made, and unto the house of the mighty. After him repaired the Levites, Rehum the son of Bani. Next unto him repaired Hashabiah, the ruler of the half part of Keilah, in his part. After him repaired their brethren, Bavai the son of Henadad, the ruler of the half part of Keilah.

schools.summary: Delitzsch notes the register's formula changing from at his hand to after him, puts the wall opposite the royal sepulchres on the eastern side of Zion following Thenius, and takes the brethren for the inhabitants of the second half-district; Ellicott places the sepulchres on the western side of the Temple and concedes they have never been traced, identifies the pool with Hezekiah's reservoir and the house of the mighty with David's picked troops, and marks the circuit coming round toward the Temple.
Gill supplies that Beth-zur was a strong fortified place in Judah, and leaves the brethren open between the kinsmen of the two men named and the Levites at large, as Jarchi has it.
Clarke passes on Calmet's identification of the pool with Hezekiah's siege reservoir and takes the house of the mighty for a guard post or the city watch.

debates.question: Where were the sepulchres of David?

positions.position: On the eastern side of Zion, with an entrance to the royal tomb there
Excavated on the western side of the Temple, and never yet traced
The inhabitants of the second half-district, under the other ruler
Either the kinsmen of the two men named, or the Levites in general

outliers.claim: Concedes that the royal sepulchres, the chapter's firmest-sounding landmark, have never been located at all.

themes: After him repaired Nehemiah the son of Azbuk, the ruler of the half part of Beth–zur, unto the place over against the sepulchres of David, and to the pool that was made, and unto the house of the mighty.
After him repaired the Levites, Rehum the son of Bani. Next unto him repaired Hashabiah, the ruler of the half part of Keilah, in his part.
After him repaired their brethren, Bavai the son of Henadad, the ruler of the half part of Keilah.

19.pericope_label: And next to him repaired Ezer the son of Jeshua, the ruler of Mizpah, another piece over against the going up to the armoury at the turning of the wall. After him Baruch the son of Zabbai earnestly repaired the other piece, from the turning of the wall unto the door of the house of Eliashib the high priest. After him repaired Meremoth the son of Urijah the son of Koz another piece, from the door of the house of Eliashib even to the end of the house of Eliashib.

schools.summary: Delitzsch reads the armoury as an abbreviation of house of arms and declines to place it precisely, denies that the adverb can mean anger and takes it as emulation, and refuses Bertheau's conjectural reading up the hill on the ground that localities always follow the verb in this narrative; Ellicott renders the phrase the armoury of the corner and puts it at the north-west corner of the city of David, reads the adverb as emulation, and admits he cannot explain the man's motive.
Gill takes the adverb at its root as anger, with Baruch angry at the backwardness shown to the work, and notes that Meremoth had already finished an earlier portion before starting this one.

Clarke keeps the armoury's function rather than its site, a tower defending the angle or the city arsenal, and reads the adverb as plain zeal; Wesley infers from the measurement that the door of the high priest's house stood at one end and not in the middle.
Henry reads the zeal without rivalry, the man being the most vigorous rather than the others cold, and gathers the pattern of builders taking a second share where the need was greatest.

debates.question: What does the adverb rendered earnestly mean?

positions.position: Anger: he was angry at the backwardness shown to the work
Emulation or contending, not anger at all
Plain zeal and activity, without either anger or rivalry

debates.question: Where was the armoury at the turning of the wall?

positions.position: Probably the east side of Zion, or an angle within the city; it cannot be stated precisely
The north-west corner of the city of David, with its own wall
Either a tower defending the angle or the city arsenal where weapons were kept

outliers.claim: Infers the architecture from the measurement: since the wall is reckoned first to the door of the high priest's house and then to its end, the door stood at one end rather than in the middle.

themes: And next to him repaired Ezer the son of Jeshua, the ruler of Mizpah, another piece over against the going up to the armoury at the turning of the wall.
After him Baruch the son of Zabbai earnestly repaired the other piece, from the turning of the wall unto the door of the house of Eliashib the high priest.
After him repaired Meremoth the son of Urijah the son of Koz another piece, from the door of the house of Eliashib even to the end of the house of Eliashib.

22.pericope_label: And after him repaired the priests, the men of the plain. After him repaired Benjamin and Hashub over against their house. After him repaired Azariah the son of Maaseiah the son of Ananiah by his house. After him repaired Binnui the son of Henadad another piece, from the house of Azariah unto the turning of the wall, even unto the corner. Palal the son of Uzai, over against the turning of the wall, and the tower which lieth out from the king’s high house, that was by the court of the prison. After him Pedaiah the son of Parosh.

schools.summary: Delitzsch argues that the plain means the Jordan valley and not the country round Jerusalem, so that priests were then living near Jericho, and attaches the word high to the tower rather than to the king's house because no upper and lower royal house is known; Ellicott identifies the plain as the Kikkar, renders the phrase the high tower outlying from the palace, and fixes the corner at the north-eastern angle of the city of David.
Gill leaves the plain open between Jericho and the country round the city, and notes that Palal lived at the turning of the wall and so repaired what stood before him.
Clarke places the plain round about Jerusalem, where the singers and other temple officers dwelt.

debates.question: Where did the priests of the plain live?

positions.position: In the Jordan valley, probably near Jericho
In the plain country round about Jerusalem, with the singers
Either, without deciding

debates.question: Does high belong to the tower or to the king's house?

positions.position: To the tower: nothing is known of an upper and lower royal house, and the same tower is later called the great tower
To the tower, rendered the high tower outlying from the king's palace

outliers.claim: Reports without embarrassment that nothing further is known of Benjamin, Hashub or Azariah, and declines to place the corner on a compass point.

themes: And after him repaired the priests, the men of the plain.
After him repaired Benjamin and Hashub over against their house. After him repaired Azariah the son of Maaseiah the son of Ananiah by his house.
After him repaired Binnui the son of Henadad another piece, from the house of Azariah unto the turning of the wall, even unto the corner.
Palal the son of Uzai, over against the turning of the wall, and the tower which lieth out from the king’s high house, that was by the court of the prison. After him Pedaiah the son of Parosh.

26.pericope_label: Moreover the Nethinims dwelt in Ophel, unto the place over against the water gate toward the east, and the tower that lieth out. After them the Tekoites repaired another piece, over against the great tower that lieth out, even unto the wall of Ophel. From above the horse gate repaired the priests, every one over against his house.

schools.summary: Delitzsch treats the Nethinim verse as a remark inserted where the wall reaches Ophel, places the water gate beyond the south-eastern corner of the temple area against Bertheau, supplies the building history of Ophel's wall under Jotham and Manasseh, and seeks the horse gate in the wall crossing the Tyropoeon valley with Thenius; Ellicott makes Ophel the rounded spur south of the Temple and holds that nothing is said of the Nethinim's part in the work, and corrects the plural after them to after him.
Gill takes Ophel for a high tower on the wall and reads the verse as recording that the Nethinim repaired where they lived, and offers three derivations of the horse gate's name.
Clarke keeps the horse gate to the watering of horses and places it near the temple; Wesley notes that the Tekoites finished their first share sooner than others did theirs.

debates.question: Did the Nethinim work on the wall?

positions.position: Yes: they repaired at Ophel because that was where they lived
No: nothing whatever is said of their part in the general labour
The verse is a parenthesis about their dwellings, inserted where the wall reaches their quarter
A high tower standing on the wall at this point
The long rounded spur of ground running south of the Temple

outliers.claim: Explains how two quite different stretches of wall can both be described as opposite the great tower, since the tower stood well inside the city wall.

themes: Moreover the Nethinims dwelt in Ophel, unto the place over against the water gate toward the east, and the tower that lieth out.
After them the Tekoites repaired another piece, over against the great tower that lieth out, even unto the wall of Ophel.
From above the horse gate repaired the priests, every one over against his house.

29.pericope_label: After them repaired Zadok the son of Immer over against his house. After him repaired also Shemaiah the son of Shechaniah, the keeper of the east gate. After him repaired Hananiah the son of Shelemiah, and Hanun the sixth son of Zalaph, another piece. After him repaired Meshullam the son of Berechiah over against his chamber. After him repaired Malchiah the goldsmith’s son unto the place of the Nethinims, and of the merchants, over against the gate Miphkad, and to the going up of the corner. And between the going up of the corner unto the sheep gate repaired the goldsmiths and the merchants.

schools.summary: Delitzsch denies that Shemaiah is the descendant of David of that name, insists the east gate is the temple's and not the water gate, refuses to infer that the keeper fortified his own gate, sets out both ways of dividing the obscure closing sentence, and concludes from the closed circuit that the forty-two sections describe the entire wall without a gap; Ellicott identifies Shemaiah with the descendant of David, reads the house rather than the place of the Nethinim, and can say nothing at all about the gate Miphkad.
Gill states the arithmetic of the sixth son, notes that Malchiah was named from the goldsmiths' trade, and observes that the building ends where it began.

Clarke shows the versions cannot agree what the two trades were, the Syriac making them goldsmiths and druggists, the Arabic smelters and porters, the Greek copies dividing between merchants and sellers of shields; Wesley turns the sixth son into a maxim, that in doing good we need not wait for our betters to go first.
Henry makes the younger brother who serves his generation the better gentleman, and takes the man who repaired before his chamber for a lodger doing his part.

debates.question: Who was Shemaiah the keeper of the east gate?

positions.position: The descendant of David of that name in the older genealogy
Hardly that man, and the second candidate is excluded too; the identification is open

debates.question: How should the obscure closing sentence be divided?

positions.position: By the Masoretic pointing, so that Malchiah repairs the whole stretch
As the house of the Nethinim, with the traders delivering there what they brought for worshippers

outliers.claim: Suggests the eastern wall of the temple area needed least restoration because it suffered less in the Chaldean demolition, or had been partly repaired when the temple was rebuilt.

themes: After them repaired Zadok the son of Immer over against his house. After him repaired also Shemaiah the son of Shechaniah, the keeper of the east gate.
After him repaired Hananiah the son of Shelemiah, and Hanun the sixth son of Zalaph, another piece. After him repaired Meshullam the son of Berechiah over against his chamber.
After him repaired Malchiah the goldsmith’s son unto the place of the Nethinims, and of the merchants, over against the gate Miphkad, and to the going up of the corner.
And between the going up of the corner unto the sheep gate repaired the goldsmiths and the merchants.
